lead: An actuator turns an electrical command into motion or force. A sensor listens to the world; an actuator changes it. The command may be a simple on or off, as with a relay, or a precise position, as with a motor. The motor type decides whether the motion is precise, fast or cheap. Actuators open water valves in a smart home, move robot arms, position printer heads and drive the wheels of a delivery robot. This chapter groups actuators by energy source and then explains the motors that most syllabi name.
prereq: You need 2.1 for the sensor side of the feedback loop.

blocks.text: An actuator is a device that converts an input signal, usually electrical, into controlled motion or force. It is the output side of an IoT node. A sensor measures temperature, light or position and produces a signal; an actuator takes a signal and produces a physical change. In a feedback loop the sensor checks what the actuator did (see 2.1).

Group actuators by energy source. Electrical actuators use a motor, solenoid or heater. Pneumatic actuators use compressed air; hydraulic actuators use oil pressure. Thermal actuators use expansion, as in a bimetallic strip. Magnetic actuators use a coil and a magnet. Electrical actuators dominate IoT because they run from low voltage and are easy to switch.

A solenoid is a coil that pulls a plunger when current flows. It gives short linear motion, on or off. A relay is a solenoid that moves contacts: a small coil current controls a larger load circuit. Both are on-off actuators, not positioners. Pneumatic and hydraulic valves need sizing for flow and pressure; only a few universities examine that, so this chapter stays with electrical motors.

A brushless DC (BLDC) motor has a permanent-magnet rotor and fixed stator windings. There are no brushes. The stator current must change direction as the rotor turns, or the torque falls to zero. Hall sensors or a back-EMF estimate tell the driver the rotor position. The driver switches the three stator phases in sequence; this is electronic commutation.

Six-step drive turns two phases on at a time and gives six current states per electrical cycle. It is simple and common. Sinusoidal drive gives smoothly varying phase currents and produces less torque ripple and less noise. Either way the motor needs a driver with power switches, not just a DC voltage. A BLDC is efficient, has a high torque-to-weight ratio and is used in drones, fans, e-bikes and pumps.

blocks.where: f is the electrical frequency in hertz, p is the number of magnetic poles, and n is the rotor speed in rpm.

sections.h3: Stepper motor: steps and lost steps

blocks.text: A stepper motor moves in fixed angular steps. A variable-reluctance stepper has a soft-iron rotor with teeth and a wound stator. A hybrid stepper has a permanent-magnet rotor with two cups and teeth; it is the common 1.8° motor. The step angle is set by rotor teeth and stator phases.

blocks.where: θ_step is the full-step angle in degrees, N_r is the number of rotor teeth, and s is the number of steps per electrical cycle.

blocks.text: A 1.8° hybrid has 50 rotor teeth, a tooth pitch of 360/50 = 7.2°, and 4 steps per electrical cycle; 7.2/4 = 1.8°. Holding torque is the torque needed to turn the shaft while one phase is energised. Detent torque is the small torque from the permanent magnet with no current. Microstepping splits each full step into smaller current levels; 1/8 microstepping gives 0.225° per microstep for a 1.8° motor. A stepper is often run open loop: the controller counts pulses and assumes the shaft followed. If the load torque is too high or acceleration too fast, it loses steps without reporting an error. Use a servo or add an encoder when position must be guaranteed.

A servo motor is a motor with a closed loop. A DC servo has a brushed or brushless DC motor plus an encoder. An AC servo uses a synchronous AC motor plus an encoder or resolver. The drive compares commanded position with measured position and adjusts current. It can hold position under load and produces torque in all four quadrants of the torque-speed plane: forward motoring, reverse motoring, forward braking and reverse braking.

Selection in words: torque at the needed speed, load inertia, duty cycle, accuracy, cost and controller. A stepper is cheap and holds position without feedback at low speed. A BLDC is efficient and fast but needs commutation. A servo is accurate and can correct errors but costs more. A relay is best for on-off loads such as a lamp or a valve. Driving these motors from a board is covered in Unit 4, Interfacing sensors and actuators with boards.

figure.caption: A 1.8° stepper on a 2 mm lead screw: each full step moves 10 µm, and each 1/8 microstep (0.225°) moves 1.25 µm.

spec.title: Stepper + 2 mm lead screw
spec.aria: A vertical flow: a 1.8° full step gives 200 steps per revolution; with a 2 mm lead screw each full step moves 10 µm; a 1/8 microstep is 0.225° and moves 1.25 µm.

examples.question: A hybrid stepper has a step angle of 1.8° and drives a lead screw of pitch 2 mm. (a) How many steps per revolution? (b) How much linear travel per step? (c) With 1/8 microstepping, what is the resolution in degrees and in micrometres?
steps: Lead-screw pitch p = 2 mm per revolution.
Linear travel per full step = p ÷ N = 2 mm ÷ 200 = 0.01 mm.
Microsteps per revolution = 200 × 8 = 1600. Travel per microstep = 2000 µm ÷ 1600 = 1.25 µm.
examples.answer: 200 steps per revolution, 0.01 mm (10 µm) per full step, 0.225° per microstep, and 1.25 µm per microstep at 1/8 microstepping.
examples.check:
step_angle = 1.8
pitch_mm = 2.0
micro = 8
steps_rev = 360 / step_angle
travel_step_mm = pitch_mm / steps_rev
travel_step_um = travel_step_mm * 1000
micro_angle = step_angle / micro
microsteps_rev = steps_rev * micro
travel_micro_um = (pitch_mm * 1000) / microsteps_rev
print(steps_rev)
print(travel_step_mm)
print(travel_step_um)
print(micro_angle)
print(travel_micro_um)

traps: A stepper can lose steps with no error; a servo uses feedback and reports following error. Do not call an open-loop stepper a servo.
A 1.8° step angle is the full-step angle; microstepping divides it. It is not the resolution by itself.
A BLDC cannot run from a fixed DC voltage. The driver must commutate the phases.
Holding torque is with current on; detent torque is with current off. Do not swap them.
A relay coil and its contact are separate circuits; the coil is the low-power input, the contact switches the load.

quiz.a: An actuator converts an input signal, usually electrical, into controlled motion or force.

quiz.q: Why does a BLDC motor need a driver rather than a plain DC supply?
quiz.a: The stator current must change direction as the rotor turns. The driver switches the phases in sequence using rotor position from Hall sensors or back-EMF.

quiz.q: A 1.8° stepper drives a lead screw of pitch 4 mm. Find steps per revolution and linear travel per step in mm.
quiz.a: Steps per revolution = 360 ÷ 1.8 = 200. Travel per step = 4 mm ÷ 200 = 0.02 mm.

quiz.q: A machine repeats the same move and suddenly drifts. Give one likely cause if it uses a stepper, and why a servo would not drift silently.
quiz.a: The stepper likely lost steps because load torque or acceleration exceeded its ability, and open-loop control did not detect it. A servo measures position with an encoder and corrects the error, so it reports a following error instead of drifting silently.

quiz.q: State the difference between holding torque and detent torque.
quiz.a: Holding torque is the torque needed to turn the shaft while a phase is energised. Detent torque is the small torque from the permanent magnet with no current.

quiz.q: With 1/16 microstepping, what is the microstep angle of a 1.8° stepper?

Choose between a relay, a stepper and a servo for (a) switching a 230 V lamp, (b) moving a camera slider to marked positions without feedback, (c) holding a robot joint against a changing load. Give one reason each.
quiz.a: (a) Relay: it switches a high-voltage load from a low-power coil. (b) Stepper: it gives repeatable steps without an encoder. (c) Servo: it uses feedback to hold position and correct errors under changing load.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial drives add field-oriented control, which controls stator current in two axes for smoother torque. Integrated smart actuators pack a motor, driver, encoder and fieldbus into one unit. Research looks at sensorless control and printed actuators. Search terms: electronic commutation, six-step drive, microstepping, four-quadrant drive, servo sizing.
